blocks.x: For more information visit www.fema.org Thank you.
Okay, it's going again. You were talking about this band, Louis Dumaine.
Yeah.

So, anyhow, I had those, I got the music, I'd buy a whole lot of music, so, Tingaling, and, let's see, you had the Sheik, I had the Sheik, about right there, I had, well, I had a whole lot of numbers, so they would hire me, because they were too tight to buy music, and I had all the music, you see, so, Frankie played the Tramon, I don't know if you read or not, but this was in the band, Frankie Doocy.
I never knew him, yeah.

You could spell him, Tramon, but he could play like the devil. Yeah, that's what I heard, he couldn't read much. He wasn't much of a reader, so Frank played the Tramon and the Louis Dumaine, the trumpet, and that's what I told you about, the Clampy Clampy, he played the saxophone, what his name was then? He played the John Robichaud. McCurdy. He played the, and we had, let's see what else is in that band, it's a long time, and now it's hard for me to tell who played Ketor in the band, because I, for piano, I couldn't tell, it's been a long time. And so anyhow, that's about the ones I could think of, you know, we'd play all around, and that was a pretty good help for me, you know, because playing them clients that used to stick out, the clients that made you stick out, if you just jumped in and play them, you had to stick out in the band because it was wrote that way. And we played a while, so we're leaving that band, fooling around, I got with, uh, and then, uh, but he had a job at, uh, Cabaret Chef for Beans and Furry. So he says, uh, but I was playing Clampy, he said, wasn't no saxist Clampy. I said, Manny, I want you to play with me. I said, I can't afford to play with you. He said, I bought saxophone every night. I said, I don't know if I can make it. I was selling a lot to them for Paul Locker. I said, all right, all I want you to do is get a saxophone. I said, I ain't going to play that thing and turn up with all the noise in my face. I said, get a saxophone and you got the job. You're going to make an audition. You sit the clarinet, play the clarinet, sit the sax. You can see it every now and then. You can see it every now and then. You can see it every now and then. You can see it every now and then. As long as they see it, I can get the job. That was Betty Petit. Betty Petit. There was a rehearsal. My brother was in the band with Louis DeMaine and they had the Jolly 08. Joe Holler was playing bass horn. They were using bass horn. That was Clarence? Clarence was playing banjo. Did any of your other brothers play? What bass? Yeah. Any other person played? Yeah, only three of us. Clarence, and myself. I played. Yeah. Clarence played bass and Clarence. He played bass. Is Percy still living? Yeah, he stays in Detroit. He'll be in about a couple of weeks with him now, maybe a week or two. He'll be around you. You'll see him. He's going to come here on a vacation. He's a little younger than you. He's younger than Clarence. The baby brother. He's a baby. Yeah, he would play with all those bands. Jay McShane. I don't want to tell you his history. You'll have to tell it to you. Yeah. Because he played with Red Alton boys. I played in the band too when he was kids with Red Alton. That's why they hired him to play through me. Oh yeah. So, it was around the corner of the hoist.
You're a buddy of the peace band, huh?

Yeah, it was around the corner of the hoist band with Louis Deming. So, I said, now I'm going to get a saxophone. So, Joe heard about us. Joe said, Joe said, came to the house. He said, man, do you want a saxophone? I heard. I said, yeah, but I ain't got the money to buy nothing. He said, you come up to the house tomorrow and bring any kind of money you want to bring. I'll get your saxophone if you worry about that. So, I went up there and the boy Larry, Larry, he had a saxophone because he must have failed on it, couldn't play it or nothing. So, they wanted it. I guess Joe must have made something. He said, I want $50 for him. I said, yeah? He said, well, I ain't got that. He said, what you got? I said, I got $20. He said, well, just give me the $20 and pay when you get ready to play any kind of this, any old thing when you get ready. You get something, they just keep going. So, I take my saxophone and brought it on down. The night we went out there and we made an audition to see the saxophone there. I didn't play it, but I brought it out there and I played the clarinet. Then, buddy, he began to talk every time they talk about, talk about something else. We got the job. So, I played out there. We had Chani playing with us. The drummer, the drummer. Chani with Sadie. She went to New York.
I know Billy Goodson was her name, I guess. From Pensacola. Sadie? What was the name? I don't know. That's Ken. Didi. Didi's wife.

Didi's wife's sister. She was our fan. I played Sadie. This fella played banjo. I'll get his name. He stood up to town. I'll call his name after a while. My buddy was on the trumpet and I was on the clarinet trying to be on the drum. I can't call his name either. Sanji. Sanji. I don't know if his French name was Sanji. He played the guitar. You'll ask somebody else about him. They'll tell you about Sanji. He played banjo. He spoke a whole lot of Creole. He was bigger than you and he was a bunch of light-skinned. He was nice. He was pretty nice. He was a banjo player. Buddy drank so much up in there that they didn't know what he was making with the tips. The women wouldn't sing and they'd run to the bathroom and Sadie run right behind them. Whack up the money. When they came with us, they had about two, three dollars. They picked that up like it was down half. Buddy said what Sanji said, we're going to make you manager of the band. He put the law down on them. Buddy said, I ain't got nothing to do with the band no more. The band is not mine. It's out of my hand now. There's new rule in the band. If you all sing, he would tell you what to do. I said, now if you all want to sing, you sing and when you finish singing, don't go to the bathroom. Come to the music stand and we'll whack up the money. If you want to go to the bathroom, go in. Then we begin. We're going home with a dollar or 75 cents, but after that, we're going with three, four dollars a piece because they go in the bathroom and they...
They put them in their stocking and reserve.

That's right. Cut the money, put it in their chest. All the paper money is gone a few little quarters. Well, we kept that until they closed down the cabaret. When they closed down the cabaret... Where was that you were playing? Franklin and Iverville. The entertainers.
The entertainers. Yeah. 101, they called it. Well, anyhow.

Two, three people had it. That's when Beansy had it. It took five of them. Beansy, Folio, Mika, Big John. Caris Pritch used to hang around there. Five of them had it at one club. So Beansy got in with that story. That story. So he said to me, I went around, he was looking for me. He said, Manny, I want your band to play. Play over here at that story. Got a job, he'll rehearse him. I mean, advertise on Sundays and play three or four times a week. I said, well, I'm not playing. He said, I want you to get Buddy Petit. I said, uh, it's out. I said, I cannot play with Buddy Petit because I done joined Rene's band, Kid Rene. So I said, I'll tell you what I'll do. He said, well, I don't care who you got. Just come on here and get the job. I said, well, I'll get Rene because it's his band. It's not mine. So I got Rene and we went over there and run behind me and we got him one day and set up, we got the job. Get Rene signed a contract. I thought, because his band wasn't mine, but it was my job. So we stood on that job. And so he got, one time we had William for playing with us. We had six pieces. We had six or seven pieces. We had a son Chester playing bass.
We had Chester's artists.

Yeah, Chester playing bass. We had some, some, some, Thomas playing banjo. We had Edna Mitchell. We called Edna Francis. We married that boy. Edna Mitchell playing piano. You know Albert Francis, his wife. She had up playing piano. And I was on the clarinet. And I was on the saxophone. We had George Lewis on the clarinet. I played sax and George Lewis on the clarinet. And then after they had, who had played? We had Morris French playing primal. I'm making a note here about Albert Francis' wife. Edna Mitchell. Yeah, that was before. She was a step for Mitchell. We interviewed Albert Francis once, but I don't know if we didn't see his wife. I talked to her though. She must be pretty. She's a little skinny brown skin woman. I don't remember her.
She had to remember her.

She had to remember her. She had to remember her. We played there with Louis and Paul Dominguez and them. She was the one playing the piano with them. Well anyhow that was the band we played then. We advertised and then George Lewis was the town that played. Later on of course we were going to get some other jobs, some other places. But that's where I was studying.
George was in Japan. Yeah.

So George played every job Rene played. His wife would only have $6 for Rene, $1 for the leader, $5 for the men. That's where when he got $6 we got $5. His wife would sign the contract and Rene didn't get none of that money. So when he played he had to owe George Lewis $2. He owed the time one player $2. That's where Morris French put the band. He owed him a long time. His brother owed $2-$3. He owed a dollar. Son Thomas. Always in trouble but he couldn't owe me nothing because I had too many children.
That's how.

At 16 I got 11 living. So we played together. Later on then the job kind of came out and we went and played down by the alley. I put my brother in the band August too. I got August in that band with a given name. I know we played up there. So later on we pulled around and see what we did that job. That's right. We got out the band, me and August. So they went playing down by the alley. I wonder if you could tell me some more about that alley because that's right next to the St. Bernard market. Yeah. Well I didn't play down there but Rene took the job and he enjoyed it.
What kind of places were there? Were there several clubs or speakeasies or what were in there?
It was a little hole in the wall, a little night club, you know, and they would play down there.
Was there just one club there they called it the alley or was there really a little alley there that put several clubs around the alley?

No, but this was that one club. Just one club. This one club. So I didn't hardly go down there but now they played down there. So I put me up a little band, distilled it at Sturias. So Rene was playing, Ed Hand in the band and Ed was so she, I think George played with them yet. So I put up a band and I had Johnny Sincere was starting with us. I got a little boy to call Shelly to play with us that was a brother-in-law, one of the trumpet players. He didn't come to me to know how to make E flat on the horn. I showed him how to make that on the trumpet. So he played, he was doing pretty good. And so we'd have Johnny Sincere over there hoisting. We're Johnny August on the bass and when it come time to get the job Johnny was gone. So I used, I had a job on the Pelican to play. So Rene said, I want you to play the Pelican and we got a job on Sunday. St. Leger had a band, a fella called St. Leger. Do you know him? No. He was a trumpet player, he was a ball player. And he had a pretty good band too. He had Kimmel playing bass in that band. He had a whole lot of those. He had a nice band. I don't know who that didn't have in the band. He used to fool with that kid, Santiago. Lester?
No, no. Burnell.

Burnell, yeah. He had a whole lot of bad chords but he could finger like the devil. He played by head. Play the way he feel like playing. So they would try to play. I played in the band a little while with them but they had this kid that he'd make all the bad chords but he could run all over the piano. He needed to take lessons. He wouldn't do it. But for that head stuff he was a bad man when he played some of your audio. So now we play it. So I went out there with my band and I played. I had started taking my sister Cecile on the piano. Not this one, she played piano too. She don't play anymore. I took her on the piano. I took Clarence on the banjo and I took August on bass. And I had a boy around her called Sumner. August used to fool the trimones. So I had to...
Eddie Summers? Yeah, Eddie. That's right. He lost a leg last year. Yeah.

So I had him go around the corner every day by August and bring the music and try to play them parts. He could play but he couldn't play none of them parts. So anyhow August broke him in on some things and he'd get them by head and he'd sit in the band and play with us. So I had, let's see, was that Willigan on a drum? You know Willigan? No. Willigan, light skinned, but he stood uptown. Willigan. Willigan.
Willigan was all... Willigan was familiar with that? Willigan? Well then I had him on the drum. I called him Willigan.
So he's a, he was a drummer.
I had George McCullum on the trumpet.

George McCullum. So George, he died. So George stood on the trumpet, played two or three jobs out there. Next time I played out there, well, I used Gilbert. George was couldn't get George. George played the last two jobs but Gilbert played the first job. Gilbert killed on the trumpet. Sam Dutray on the clarinet. George played the last two jobs, Gilbert played the first job, Gilbert Young on the trumpet, Sam Dutre on the clarinet. I had my sister Cecile on the piano and I had Sidney Fleuja. Remember Sidney Fleuja, Light Skin Pelley played guitar and banjo? He's downtown and he ain't playing anymore, call him Sidney Fleuja. He's still around. Oh yeah, but I don't think he's playing. He was on the banjo and that was a pretty nice outfit we had then. We had eight pieces up on that job. You want eight people to name?
I think we got it all. Did you name them all? I'm just making a note about him, Sidney Fleuja.
Sidney Fleuja.
You know how that's spelled?
I don't know. This fella in them all kind of ways. It's an autograph with names.
I'll ask somebody like George Gano. He might know him.
Yeah, George you know him and not only that, everybody knows Sidney Fleuja. He's a good person.
Being a banjo player he knows Creole names too.
And let's see this fella, Gilbert Young, I don't know if you know him. No, I never did know him.
Well he was a nice trumpet player.

I think he was waiting for the post office now. I don't know if you might be able to catch him. I don't know. He played out there with Ridgely and my parents used to be his old lady. So you know you can ask about Gilbert. He said Gilbert don't stay far from home. When you be out there, just ask about Gilbert Young. I thought I used to be a husband one time. Sweetheart together, live together. I shouldn't even say that. Well that's alright.
Because other people have told me that too. Yeah that's right. Yeah, about Alexis too. Yeah, Alexis coming after Rika.
That's what you got to avoid. And let's see if you talk about some other bands you want to know about. Then after they like...
Well I was going to ask you. Go ahead.

Later on it got to the point, I didn't help all them fellas on the trumpet I got out the band with. I couldn't get no trumpet players at all. They stick with me. Right up. So anyhow, what I did, I take in and... So I said I'm going to break my boys in on the trumpet. And I know they got to play with me whether they want or not. Because I'm the daddy. So I take in Morton and August. And I learned down the trumpet, how to play the trumpet. And I learned trumpet from old man Delmore. And August and Mauret, I often find all the artificial fingering. They call it artificial but it's all in the book. Yeah. And they make all them fingering three, four ways. I know all that. So he taught old man Delmore. So anyhow, I learned about them. I broke them and I learned the trumpet. Every day I'd have them practicing them running over and making them write their music. So I had my own trumpets. So then I had a big band and about... Boy went to war when he... Before he went to war, I had a big band and I had my little nephew, Clowns Ford. Do you know him?
No.
I've heard of him. He plays with Fat Domino.
Yeah, I've heard of him.

Of course he's a progressive, you know. He's not. So I had him in the band and my little boy Charles Gabriel in the band playing tenor. August playing trumpet three boys. August and Mauret. And then I used him in the brass band. I had this boy, Herbert Horace, playing high note and Henry. Henry Jarvis, he was playing tenor. I would play the Alpes, so that was four. But Alpes could play clarinet, but that Henry Jarvis, we had three clarinets we played. He could play the tenor, he couldn't play the clarinet. But about 16th piece, I used Richard McLean on the bass. Oh yeah. I used him on the banjo piano. I didn't even use this boy, Winley's brother. Not Winley the other one, Homer. Oh yeah. Homer Eugene.
Homer Eugene.

Yeah, well he played. We had a nice band and I kept up then sometime. I would give him a read section, Howard would bring me his folks. He had a big band too. Same man had Clifford Brown playing with him. Know Clifford? Yeah, I don't know him. So anyhow, he would sing and he had a nice voice. So we'd play all over. So Clifford, I got a little job for Dave Foster. About ten we played. And on the five piece, we had this fellow Joe Morris. Drum, the little boy, Lil Morris. The little drummer, he's shorty. He looked almost bigger than the midget. Well he was the drummer, Howard and all of them know him. Joe Morris. So he played drummer that was out there.
There's been a Morris, a bass player. That's his son, that's his son.

And he could sing any blues. They had the people there, but they had a, we call it armor there, you know, and a shikiro, packed up from the bottom to the top. Nothing but records. Nothing but blues. And any blues, they could say, give me a chord in B flat or a chord in C or a chord in G. And he would sing them blues out to Dave Foster. We had five pieces out there. He was Charles August, and Lil Joe, myself, and his boy Clifford Brown. He was five pieces. Now a long time before that, I played green clarinet in August. We played three pieces, just with the clarinet. Our picnics all day, this is the clarinet, the bass, and the banjo. And we got tired. We played all day, this is that clarinet, the bass, and the banjo. And when I couldn't make it with him, I had to play somebody, you should get Elliot Taylor. You ever heard of him? Oh, yes, I've heard of him.
Well, I'd get him to play in my place.

He could do the same thing with that clarinet. He need no trumpet. Play all day, a picnic. Elliot Taylor's to play in my place. We'd clean up, and that's where I'd come up the hard way, so when it comes easy, where it didn't mean a thing. When did you go to Detroit? I went to Detroit in 48. The last job I played around here was for the priests somewhere down in the Burris. But I was in that WPFN where there were 128 of us in there.
Oh, yes, I've seen a picture of that.
I've seen a picture of that. Now I'm playing in Detroit with a band, Dick and Joan. How big a band is it?
What's it like?

That's a Dixieland band. Small Dixieland? Not small, but I call it big Dixieland. Oh, big Dixieland. It's six pieces. They was playing the state fast, so. You play clarinet? Oh, yes, that's what I play.
I wonder if you played sax or mostly clarinet or what was it?

I got to lay on that sax, the man want Dixieland, but I got to sax to have some people want to have some monkey shine. Well, it's a different story. You can read the letter. Oh, yes. See what it's talking? Yonkers, that's New York. Yeah. I think that's a little letter in there.
You can read it out. He wants me to play now.

I couldn't play now. I'm going to retire and I'll be with him. You can read it out and put that on if you want to. That's all right. I'll just look over it in the other hand. This is from Deacon Jones, he calls it. That's right. They play at the World's Fair. Two weeks, yes. Oh, are you working at Ford?

Yeah, I'm a little tired September. That's what I want to do. Will you stay up there, come back here, do you think? I'm not trying to get nosy into your fair. I know, but if I play with him, see I want to do it. Yeah. Oh, yes. He'll pay me $25 a night and $35 on Sunday. On Sunday, you see. They go to Albany and you see.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Oh yeah, I'm into music, I never stopped playing. I played with my boy, my boy's got a contract he signed up for here in Portland, Orphan. Charles Gabriel, my little boy's playing the Orphan over there. But anyhow, that's the job that I have there. Now we played all over, we played at the Parkland Hotel for two years. Two years we played at Parkland Hotel. I think I showed you that, didn't I?
No, I didn't see that.
Oh yeah. Two years we played at Parkland, supposed to play two weeks, and I broke them in on the Dixieland because they wanted Dixieland. Then the man said it would be something different.

They call that the Cats and Jammer. That's right, Cats and Jammer. The Parkland Cocktails. That's nice. Well I was going to ask about Freddie Keppard, if you could tell a little bit more about him. You knew him when he first started then?
Well, on the air, I knew him before he was playing violin. He used to play violin with my daddy, Freddie. Freddie Keppard and Louis Keppard is around.

Yeah, he's still here. I know him quite well. Well, yeah. I never did get to meet his brother. I have some of his records, Freddie's records. Never met Louis? Oh, Louis, I know. But not Freddie. Freddie died before I got...

Well, Freddie went to Chicago, looking book 1910. He went to Chicago 1910. Him and my impressed never could get along together. So when I went... Do you know where he took lessons or what he did? With R.C. Bia. That's all I can tell you. R.C. Bia. Freddie Keppard took lessons from R.C. Bia on the trumpet. Now the violin, I couldn't tell you who taught him because I wouldn't know anything about that. But the trumpet, he took lessons from R.C. Bia on the... He was a top trumpet player too. Always could read the music. All he'd get to ping and then the rip and he was gone. So he made history on that trumpet in 1910. He went to Chicago. So that's the only man Benny Goodman talked about Freddie Keppard. He don't talk about Louis Armstrong, even Joe Alvon.
He was up there before then.
Yeah, he was ten years. The job was there in 1923.
See, that's when Louis Armstrong went there.

And the last thing Louis played was a dance for my daddy at the Coliseum. I advertised, not the dance. He played the advertised. I played the clarinet. He left that same night in 1923. First time a dance was ever gave down there. But Sidney Dazman, he played the job. And I played with Sidney Dazman's band, two drums. He just came into me and I played the drum in the band. When I was playing the drum in the band, I was on the drum. Vic was on the tramo, Vic Gasper. And Sidney Dazman on the trumpet. The crew on the clarinet. Willie Vaughn 10 on the banjo. And Oak was on the bass. Is that six pieces? I think so. Well, that was that band I played with them. And when we played that high society, we had to get very low for Piku. And we played all those places around. I was a drum in that band. But Sidney was playing by himself in grown lady years. And he put up a big band where he could sit behind the axe and do nothing. But he used to play a nice trumpet. And Joe Oliver, when we would be rehearsing, he would come and rehearsing with my dad. He couldn't leave a number. King Oliver. He clubbed with a cataract now. You ever seen him? I know, but I was seeing the picture.
I know he had the one bad eye.
Yeah, well, alright. Well, he would be in the club. So after rehearsing with us a whole lot and playing a little round, Bruce the man was playing peck horn then.
Oh really?

He was a good trumpet player. And so he played. And Michael Perez taking him in the band. And after he got through the orchestra with Kid Orwell, he was fast. He always heard that monkey shine. And he went up the line. He sent him out of scrum. There was a whole lot of fellas around here that could play old time fellas. Such as, you know Suga? No. That was a time I wanted to play over the river. Jack Pyee? No.
A lot of those people.
Well, all that you could have got from Peter Bocas. I don't see why they didn't give it. Maybe he mentioned it.
Peter Bocas could give you all those colors. We did interview him. He talked for quite a while. Then he told him. I forgot the name for him.
Well, Suga was over there. Jack Pyee. And Buddy Johnson. And Mr. That other fella. Did you tell anything about George McCullum? Yeah. I don't mean the boy. I'm talking about the daddy.
I have a good picture of him too. Yeah, the old man and the boy.
We talked to his widow.
It was still over in the project. Not far from where it is. The old man?
The old lady?

The old lady. That's been about three years since I saw her. She still had his horn. A little short con. Cornet. I got an E flat. I think she's giving it to the museum maybe. I got an E flat conet too.
About that big. E flat.
His was B flat but it was one of those little short ones.
I got one of them. I got an E flat. E flat conet. And I got a B flat conet. And so I mean that's in Detroit. I got my E flat clarinet chair with me too. But I'm not.
Oh yeah, you still have your E flat. Did you ever play many parades in the old days? Well I played. I'm a member of the Ricker band.
I got T-Boy with me. I was a member of the Ricker band. Oh yes.
Yeah I used to play this. I remember when T-Boy was the manager. T-Boy.

Well I'm in that X-Squad with him. You see X-Squad book you'll see Manny Gabriel. I'm playing saxophone not clarinet. Because we used Piku. When Piku didn't play then I played or John Cash. I played the saxophone. If they were short of the drummer I played the drums. Yeah. The Albert system too.
That's right.
Fordham's album.
Yeah. That's right. I guess just about everybody used Albert here.
Yes what they used at them time. I still use the album.
Still good. Still good. I think they have better tone in the band system.
Yeah I think so too.
Bigger, fuller tone. More mellow or something.
Then I got another E flat from Germany. I think the kids ruined them out. It's a mouthpiece.
Is it Albert? It's Albert too. It's Albert from Germany.
But it's smaller. It's smaller in here. Yeah. And the mouthpiece is smaller. Small all together.
Is it in tune the right pitch or is it higher?
It's the right pitch and everything they said at mouthpiece. Just the smaller one.
It's good shape too.
What they make?
Is it buffet or something? I don't know. I don't know what it is.

I got a buffet ground it over at the house but it's got a crack in it. And so, but I still got it to be ground it. It's hard to get them buffets. Especially now but I can get a buffet in there. Bam, but you can't get them. It's hard to get them.
No, they don't make the Albert touch anymore like that. So.

That's a nice little case for it too. I was going to play that parade when I'm sunny but she didn't ring me up so I didn't go. I wasn't going to go running behind them. I told them to call me up. Yeah, it's too bad. But he didn't call me so I was going to play the parade just to be playing. I understand. So yeah. I want to come out of there. I'll get out there after a while. There's music or nothing?
No, no.

That's just to read. Oh, I read them. I mean a box with the reader. I'll get it out there. Anyhow, we played a record band. I played all around with T-Boy and me. We even played. We played the Chum Club. I can't exactly tell you. When I was in the WPA band I can't tell you what year that was because I don't know if it was 1930 or 1933 or 34. I don't know what it was. But anyhow, when I was at WPA I was playing Big Carous Chum Club. T-Boy was playing trumpet. We had Sam Lee playing tenor. Sam Lee, we didn't have a time on it. We had a boy they called Benny Tony from over the river.
He was playing piano. Yeah, he was playing piano.

I was playing the clarinet in the alto. Sam played the tenor in the clarinet. We had Sidney Fusier playing the ghetto or banjo. He could change either one. We would play there every night. We would come on there at 1030. Babe Carous Chum Club, Decayden Toulouse. That was our bunch. We had Roy playing drummer. The boy they called Roy. He stood uptown somewhere named Roy Evans. I think he was. Oh, I've heard of him. He died. Well, that was our drummer. Then we had the barrica band. We would play all them funerals, parade in the band. They had John Cashman. He was a clarinet player. I could play sax with him. See? And he played the clarinet. Couldn't touch the clarinet. He didn't want that. So we played the clarinet. We had Ray playing bass. But it's red, big red. You know Ray? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And Ray playing with, we had Tillman playing trumpet with us sometime. And Ray Park was that?
Yeah.
And you played trombone for a while. Yeah. And then we had this fellow, big tall fellow played trombone. Warner. Oh, Albert Warner.
Albert Warner. And Ray.

Sometimes Ray played the trombone. And when he didn't, then we'd use what you call them on the bass. But then after getting Ray on the bass, Warner played trombone and then we'd use what you call them on the bass. Warner played trombone and I can't call his name, but he played trombone, had two trombone players.
One time Carnish was in the band. No. That was earlier.
Yeah. That's a long time ago, but I'm talking about lately. When T-Boy had the band, Cornish wasn't in the band.
No.
We had Ray, Trimone, Trimone and his boy Trimone and Tillman played.
Oh, Sonny Henry maybe. Sonny Henry we had. Yeah, we had Sonny Henry playing. And we had a baritone player.

His brother they called, he made up that band. His brother made up that Arrica band. He played. One of the fellow Wilson. Wilson, that's it. His brother played the baritone. I can't call his name. I never knew it. But he played baritone in the band. They didn't use no peck horn. They always go saxophone to play. How to build an Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland
Okay, I see you were just finishing up about the Eureka Band, I guess.

Eureka Band, well, in our T-Boy, he was a trumpet, and like I say, the trumpet was where the little Jim playing bass from. I'm getting to the bass from a little Jim, and they had Happy playing the snare from over the river. Bill's brother, Happy.
From who?
That was Bill Matthews. Bill Matthews, you sure? Yeah, he had another room. Raymond, we call him Raymond. Yeah, he's dead now.
All of the Matthews are dead now.
Three of them, they had three. I took his brother's job at St. Morgan, that was the old one that was the game after.
They had Happy Goldston, they called him Black Happy.
Not him, he wasn't, that's not the one I'm talking about.
He was one of the last drummers, up until about two or three years ago. He had a stroke, but he's still living in, seems to get along all right.

Well, these fellas was about, his master's, he was about one of the best drummers in our lives. Oh, yeah. Him and Cantrell, well, I even learned how to, I ain't got them sticks now, but I can take them sticks and beat them up in there, just like that.
Oh, yeah, I've seen Chinese do that too.

Well, and I, I don't mean hip, one, I mean it's beat, just like I beat them, roll them down, yeah. Oh. I mean, the same thing up in there with them, but then I used to do that a long time, so I learned that from him. And another boy called Faiso, he went away from me, he beat that, he used to play a Louis Armstrong, he went away from me doing that too. Well, you know, this record band had them three trumpets, Poissy, T-Boy, and Tillman. And the trumpet players was regular in the band, and then sometimes they put Tillman on the sax when somebody don't come in, and that's the way that sax bass on, John Cashman played the clarinet.
When I first heard of you, Mika, they had Schatz. Well, yeah, we used Schatz in the band, but Schatz died, you know.

Yeah, Schatz was the trumpet player in the band, two Schatz, Schatz and T-Boy and Poissy. But then after when Schatz died, then they used Tillman. They never could use Clayton in the band because he couldn't read.
Yeah, he died, you know, a couple years ago.

Yeah, because, but we had, we would play, you know, any trumpet player could play, could read, they would hide, but they could not have to read. They would hide, but they could not use Clayton in the band, them kind of fellas.
Yeah, he didn't play in all the keys either, I don't think.

No, everything he played in the wrong key would start us up. And the record band done pretty good. There was a scab band, the record band, I'm going to tell you how it was. It was a scab band, and I belonged to the union, so they would be over at the Gypsy T-Room. When I would pass there, I had my boy playing clarinet in the band, and they wouldn't say nothing to me. I'd say, I'm teaching the band, and I'd get by with murder. Yeah. I'd pass there and I'd blow my clarinet all up in Williamson, fellas, they'd say, you know, man, it's crazy. Anybody else would do that, they'd charge him $50 a fine. Yeah. I played with another bunch of fellas from around here, a long time ago, let's see if I could come in with this bunch. I ain't never thought. Oh yeah, with the Sydney Fluesa, we had a band with Rudolph. The big Rudolph the drummer? Yeah, he played in the band Rudolph. I haven't seen him right now, I bet he's still here though. Yeah, I heard his clip of Rudolph, played a drummer, and his boy, Al Seed, played alto in the band, Al Seed. Sidney Fluesa played the banjo, and the boy they called T-Boy played bass from uptown, a little short fella called T-Boy.
Yeah, maybe.
Well anyhow, he played in the band and Gilbert Jung played trumpet, Gilbert.
Yeah.
And we had a fella called, French, Morris, you should call him. Morris, he played tramo.
Yeah, I never knew, he's up in the, oh up the river, like Laplace or Laplace or whatever they call it, someplace up there.

Not that Morris French, another one. Oh, another one. Another one, another one. Another one, huh? He stood down by that market there. Oh, oh. When he played tramo, now you talking about a fella, Norm's them brother, not him. Yeah. You ever heard of Gus, Gus Madcat? I'm not sure.
He played trumpet, baritone, he played all of them. Gus Madcat.

Baritone, trumpet, the peck horn, and the fella called White used to play in the band. And Johnny Nelson, all those was old time musicians. So he didn't know sugar. Well that little band, we kept that band up for a long time, that was six pieces. I gave him that little band up with Gilbert, named Rudolph. And I played again with a fella, Joe Petit, Ambrose. Joe Petit played Valder. Oh yeah.

He played tramo and played from there. I made a little record of him one time in his last days. He was quite deaf, he couldn't hardly hear what he was playing. But at least we had him on record so we could hear him play a little.
Well anyhow, this fella, I know you're worried of him, he played, what was Joe Petit like when you played with him?
What year was that in brass bands?
He played in orchestra too, he played all around Joe Petit. He had no teeth in his mouth, he could play.
Even when I made the record, he could still play though.

Yeah, well he played with no teeth, played the tramo with no teeth in his mouth, his mother, his buddy Petit's stepdad, he raised him and Buddy Petit took his name. But anyhow, he was pretty fair. And Ambrose, you know Ambrose you see, he was a violin player, he learned how to play tramo. And Louis Prevost, you know him? No. Well he played Clannock with Louis Armstrong when they first put up the voice band. Did you ever get that name of that band?
I know there was one Judy Singleton tells about, and then the Lydie was. And some of those that played in, Barney, Big Dog, somebody. Oh that's late, that's the late.
The Clannm Anderson's ones. But that's before that time, the voice band he ever played, they made a, they had a band, and the band consisted, I'm going to start, Joe Lindsay.
Oh I was going to say, yeah that's right, Joe Lindsay told me once about that.

Joe Lindsay, well he was the voice band, Joe Lindsay was the drummer, T-Boy, the tramo player was Robert, a boy that called Robert played tramo in the band, and Louis Armstrong on the trumpet, Joe Welsh on the violin, and T-Boy on the guitar, the trumpet player, the guitar. Oh he played guitar player, he played guitar, and Louis Prevo played clarinet, he was a violin player, he was a good trumpet player in Detroit, because Louis Prevo, that's Louis Armstrong voice clarinet player. He'd go all around with his clarinet so he could get all this jazz in here, better tone these fellas I see around here. Oh yeah better tone.
What's the last name spelled? Prevo?
Prevo, that's all I mean, Louis, Louis Prevo. He's a beautiful, I don't know if he's dead or not, but anyhow.
He's not up in Detroit then anymore?
He's here, he's here. Back there. He died down there, working boys, everyone on the corner there. That was a clarinet player, a nice clarinet player, he played nice. Remind you of T.O.
I was going to ask some more about T.O. Who were the very best clarinet players you ever heard down there? Who did you like best?

Well, I'm going to tell you, that's a hard thing to say because, but I can give you five or six good clarinet players, without putting that temper, I couldn't judge them because that's, I think T.O. was one of the T.O.
Did you hear his uncles and his father play? No, I never heard Papai and them, I never heard them.
And Basso and all them for the, and Ashil Bakay, he was a nice clarinet player, the white band.
I knew his brother, heard him on saxophone, George, in Philadelphia.

Well, I don't know about the sax, but he was a bad clarinet player around there, George. Now for that clarinet playing, they had a whole lot, that's in the music line, it was T.O., P.C. Koo, Charlie McCoy, Sam Dutre, I mean they're always good clarinet players. Louis Nelson, he's a good reader too.
Yeah, I knew him, I heard him, I made records on his record.
He was a good clarinet player, he was the Contreras, but he was good. And, uh, I'll call this fella, he's out of town now. He's a Lawrence Dewey.
Oh yes, he died a couple years ago or so.
He was a good clarinet player, he was a good clarinet player. Wade really sneaked up in there with him too. Wade was a pretty good clarinet.
Nobody knows where Wade is.
Well, I say he was, you know how he played?

I heard him, yeah, 1945. How did he play? Pretty good. Yeah, he was a good player. He hadn't been playing, he'd been working in a shipyard or something out in California during the war, and he went back to the clarinet, he sounded a little bit like Johnny Dodds. Do you remember Johnny Dodds?

Yeah, I know Johnny, he was a routine. I didn't count him. Now when I get to that class, on that kind of class was Sidney Bechet at that time, they all would play like Sidney Bechet, Johnny Dodds, Muley, Muley Bond. Well, they all could jam at that time around the same thing. It was old time, but they played in, uh, Georgie Boy. Yeah, I never knew him.
I heard about Georgie Boy.

Georgie Boy played clarinet too, he was with that bunch. What did you do? Well, uh, my other boy I never did mention too, he was in the band with my daddy. Had a good clarinet band, was Picoosecar Lunderville. What?
Lunderville.
Oh, no, no. He was the brother-in-law of Sidney Veen, clarinet, Lunderville. Oh, he was a good musician. Did you ever know Jimmy Newton? I think they called him Jimbo. Yeah, Jimbo.
Jimbo. Yeah, I know what I mean. Did he play much around here?

Oh, yeah, he used to play at Southern State, played a whole lot of clarinet, he was alright. I don't know, I couldn't bet on his music ability, I mean on the music, but I could tell you when coming out of the playing, it took a good man to move him. I knew he was just called.
He had that barrension, you see. Oh, he had a whole lot of fast fingering. Fast fingering. Fast fingering. I don't know how he was here. He was better here, because he was playing with boys.
He had one of the best read sections in Chicago, great Jimmy Noon. Yeah, I knew him up there.
We called him Jimbo.
Do you know anything about where he came from?
Because I never got to talk to him very much, maybe two minutes or so.
No, I'm going to tell you, that fellow, when he came here, he was playing with Maurice Durand. You ever heard of Maurice Durand?
Oh, yes, I met him once, down in the 9th Ward on the Duzardi extreme.

Well, I went in that band playing drums too, in that band with Maurice Durand. And Jimbo had left the band, so they took London, Willie Umphrey was playing in the band, Clarence Willie. Yeah. When Willie left, then they took London Vare in the band. London Vare, Buddy Johnson, and Maurice Durand, that was a three-blowing instrument. So, they had Green playing guitar, Green, and I think they had T-Boy on bass. And they had a couple other drums, trying to see somebody else. I know I was playing from the first place. Happy come out that band, Rayd Happy. Oh, yeah.
I never knew anything about him. You heard of him?

He was a good ragtime drummer. Well, I went in that band behind Happy, but I could play on the music, because the band was all reading music and it was just in my hand. I could jazz and play that music. So, the first piece we played, yes, we have no bananas. We have no bananas today. So, I got in that band and I played with that band and it was very nice. We'd get the jobs to go over the lake to play and we'd make on the train. Maurice was pretty straight Maurice Durand, my daddy Chris and his wife. And he was a nice fellow. He had a nice band, but I don't know. He was a fellow for a little while to go down. He wanted to go to New York, because all these men wanted to go to New York. So, I don't know what happened to him. Did he die?
Maurice, he went to California. I saw him, Professor Mineta and I went over there in 1958 and saw him, talk to him. And he died though about three or four years ago.
Yeah, well, Durand, he was a nice trumpet player.
Yeah, he was pretty straight though, I guess.
Yeah, he was straight, just like I said.
From Mineta and other people said. I never did hear him, I did hear him get his horn out and he played a few notes, you know, that's a little warm up.
Yeah, well, he was a nice trumpet player.
Had a nice tone and all. He wasn't playing anymore professionally when I heard.
And horse, we call him horse, you see the Minetas, I call him horse.
Yeah, everybody call him horse.
Well, horse, he was a nice fellow, just like to drink. He used to drink a whole lot, but he could play two trombones at one time.
Yeah, and then he plays trumpet and trombone.

But I said, no, I mean the two trumpets. Yeah, two trombones at one time, he had a stand. When Louis Armstrong came there, he had a stand and there about seven to eighteen hundred people on that store, that place was going like that. Well, he played.
He still does that.
Yeah, he played two trumpets and he played two trombones. I seen him play two trombones.
Now he plays the trombone at this hand and the trumpet at this hand. Yeah. He puts the strap around and plays the trombone and the trumpet. That's really good.

I know one thing, if this clarinet was broke, all these keys here, one or two of these keys can't come down or anything, and they just plug them up there and he'd play that clarinet just like nothing ain't happen. That's right, he was something. He'd done it with us, you know. That's all right, don't play two, three, four, five keys. Play it right on. Yeah, he was a great clarinet player. He played a whole lot of clarinet, he played a whole lot of piano, and he had the chords and trumpet. I know he could play it in the violin. He played all the instruments. He's teachers now.

Yeah, well, yeah. Although he's about retired, he doesn't do much. He's seventy-five years old now. Yeah, he ought to be around there. He was a nice-looking man when he was here. Yeah, he was a nice-looking man when he was here. Yeah, he still looks good. He was very sick a year ago, had an operation, but he pulled out of it all right and got over looks better than he did a few years ago.
And he'd go around playing for nothing with fellas just because he liked them.
Well, he said he used to go around with Maurice Duran. They'd have a little trio or just two or three of them go around and serenade people and all that. He's a nice fella.
He was very nice. That's a panza mella. Oh, yes.
It's a nice, nice husky. Looks like it's in good shape, too. You got all your keys shined up and everything.

Well, I ain't shined up, but I ain't been using it in about a couple of weeks because I stopped the fellas' money to play out there, but I couldn't make them jobs out of town. It's all right when it's playing the four-plane hotel. I have to go too far. I couldn't make it.
Yeah, not when you're working day time, don't you think?
Yeah, so everything went on.
Anything else about the old-time clarinetist you can tell about T.O. any more about how he played? Did he read a good deal, too? T.O.? Oh, oh, oh. Did he play a lot of jazz, too?

He played all kind of ways. That's about the, that is about, when I say, why I put him so high because he played at E flat, he played the B flat, he done a lot more singing than Piku. People might use the name of the B kooze all right, but that fella was a, and he was so clean. Oh, he was a clean clarinet player. I ain't never had, I never did play with him in my life, but just stand up and look at him and play. You know when something's nice, why you got to do this stand up? Well, he was in Chicago, and this fella, Donnell, do you know him? Donnell Howard?
Yeah, big fat play clarinet.

So he was playing with Earl Hines, and, because I went there to see George Foster, they were playing in Detroit, so he was telling me, he said, man, I used to look, I used to look at that old tall son, look unfair, that clarinet, and said, God, if I could only play like him, nah, that's what Donnell says, you know, he was a great clarinet player. And, uh, Wooden Joe used to play clarinet, too.
Oh yes, I knew him, they'd trumpet mostly, that way.
Yeah, the cornet he played, yeah, the cornet, Willie Phillip, you ever heard of him?
No.
He played in the band, Joe, played in the band with my daddy, too, Wooden Joe, trumpet, my daddy and Willie Phillip.
Oh, Willie Phillip played?
Trumpet.
Trumpet, too.
Yeah. Walter Blue, you ever heard of him? Yes, younger. He died.
Frank Keeling, you heard of him? Yeah, how was he? I never heard much about him, though, very little. Was he from uptown? Yeah. Somebody told me he was good on the blues, and that's the best.
Yeah.
I think it was really hard to get along with or something.
He used to fight a lot, fight. Boy of the horn don't bring him back.
And how did he play, did he read good, too, or just the most clear? He could play with anybody, he could play with anybody.
Frank Keeling, he played all in band.
How old would you say he was, or do you know when he died?
I'd give him about, I'd give him about...
Your father's age, or?

I think he was a little older than my four, I believe. I don't know, I'm giving him... Yeah. He might have beat my daddy about five or six years or four years. He was an old time. Do you know when he died or what happened to him? No, I don't know when he died because he could have died in jail for all I know. He was a bad man, he had a cucks on his face.

When would be about the last time that you heard him or that he played? Because I can't find anybody hardly that knows him. Well, the last time I was in playing, I was a kid. Just a kid, huh? Yeah, I was a good friend of mine. Maybe 1910 or along in there?
No, around 1920.
20 or 15, something or somewhere along.
Like Jimmy Strode, you never heard of him?
I've heard of him, but don't know anything about him.

Well, he was a fellow who used to play that trumpet, and he had all them got beats about him. Old man Barbara, you heard him, I'll have to tell you about him. I know you're old boy. He was a nice musician too.
Well, there was Joe Johnson. I knew Bunk Johnson very well. Did you get to hear him when you were a kid?
Yeah, I don't know. He used to play the Eagles band. He used to play a person, and he had Dave the Pass play clarinet with him, Dave. I know all the pass, that's Rudolph, his brother.
Oh yes, I knew that they were related, because I got a picture of Arnold, DuPas, Rudolph. Well, I know I played the drum.

Rudolph played the drum, but Dave played the clarinet. And those other boys, all those boys, as Moran's played music. It's like I have six boys. I have Joe, he plays bass. I have my little boy, he plays the piano and the organ. Elliot, he's been the line half for three years. I have Charles, he's played the sax, the clarinet, the flute, the baritone. I have the next one, August, he plays the trumpet, he plays the organ. I have Morton, he plays the piano and the trumpet. That's only five, short of one of them, I don't know which one. I think that's about six of them. Well, they all play. Leonard, he plays the trumpet too. It's a pretty valid tritomo, but he plays. He's young, but I mean, he plays all of them, and all of them play.
Well, there were a couple of other trumpet players on the front of my mind. Joe Johnson, do you remember him on the trumpet from uptown? Lee Collins used to tell me about it.
Yeah, Lee Collins, he used to play wrestling. He'd go to sleep on Coley. Yeah, Joe Johnson played trumpets up there.
Do you remember Joe Johnson, what he played like, or what style?

No, I can't tell you for long. I remember ragtime, not Chip. Chip was a good trumpet player, favorite kid. I remember Chip. He played bass after, but he was a trumpet player. Chip and a fellow they called Jesse. He used to get all them jobs, guitar players. Jesse.
Oh, and Tick Chambers was another trumpet player.

Yeah, he went to Chicago to go outside tomorrow and Tick Chambers was another trumpet player. He played Kedora Band too. How did he sound? Do you remember? He was a gut bucket trumpet player. The other brother that you should know, Sugar Johnny.
Yeah, I never got to knowing that.

He was a good trumpet player. Yeah, I've heard about him. I played in the band with him too, drummer. I don't play in the band with Sugar Johnny. Sugar Johnny was a nice trumpet player. He played with Roy Palmer.
I knew Roy Palmer. Roy Palmer, I played with him too.

Roy Palmer. He played trumpet and tramo. He learned Kedora Ney. People will know that, but he learned Kedora Ney a whole lot. Roy Palmer. He was right down there on the Georgia Martin corner. Roy would have him tall, skinny, dark man, Roy Palmer. He died about two years ago. He used to play in the band with my daddy, Roy Palmer. Look, it's alright if you want to stop. It's alright. Do you want to go and answer the phone? Who is it, boy, though? What were you talking about? Some trumpet players. Oh, Roy Palmer. Yeah, Roy Palmer.
Roy Palmer.
Yeah, Roy Palmer. He was nice. How to build their leg.
You know Lego? No. Don't think so. Oh, yes.
He died. He was a trumpet player too. Play trombone and baritone. Oh, Roy Palmer. Roy Palmer, he was nice. You know Lego?
No, I don't think so. You know Harrison Ball?
Oh yes. He was a trumpet player too.
He played trombone in the baritone.

When I played with Sam Baldwin, all that music Sam couldn't play, then they hired him to play it. And some trombone player played in his place, and he'd pick up the trumpet and play all them numbers that Sam couldn't play. That trombone blues and all the music, he played all the music, that man, he was a good trumpet player.
A good musician.

Yeah, and another trumpet, you ask about trumpet players, I'm trying to think of one of them fellas used to jump up to old trumpet. I know these young fellas, I know you ain't trying to worry about them.

Most of the younger fellas, we've talked to them, I'm wondering about those old timers that are dead now that we'll never know anything about unless somebody like you tells us. Yeah, or some fella tells us. Who were your favorite trumpet players? Who did you like best of all?
Well, I liked Emmanuel Peres. I liked Emmanuel Peres above all the trumpet players because…
Did he play most legitimate or did he play good jazz? He made things, everything was clean on his horn and he was powerful.

Oh, he was powerful, Joe Oliver was sounding. He made Joe Oliver stronger than Joe Oliver hold up that band but after, later on, them two would come with a brass band, you'd think it was about five or six trumpets with them two Joe Oliver and Emmanuel when they'd go pick up. They held the band up all day long.
He said that very well.
My daddy, huh?
Wish I could have heard that.

Oh, I was making the monkey shine while Emmanuel was carrying that melody, you know. And that all kind of stuff on the trumpet. And the clarinet talking, oh, the band was, that little Ricker band, I wasn't even counting with that kind of a band. And the fellas played a whole lot.
Well, how was the Keppard compared with that one?

Keppard was in there, Freddie. Oh, yeah. Freddie was a bad trumpet player too. He was powerful like Joe Oliver and I think he was a better musician, Joe Oliver, Freddie Keppard. Because he was a good violin player, see? Yeah. And the voice of music was nothing. He had that down but he just had to get the finger in the trumpet. I think it was better trumpet player than Joe Oliver. That's the one this man Benny Goodman talked about. Yeah. He had a tone like Kid Rene. Shockey Banana, you ever listen to his tone? Yeah. Yeah. Shockey. That's what I've heard, he's something like Rene.
Well, Rene learned Shockey. Yeah, he learned from Rene.

So, Rene's got a tone, something on the art of Freddie Keppard. When he was playing he had a pretty tone and he had such a fast finger in it. And he had a good lip on him. Very good lip on him. And I wouldn't come down to Jerry Rene, he was a bad man.

How did those old time bands sound compared to the ones now? Were they about the same style or different styles? The brass band, yeah. Well, I mean the dance bands I was thinking of. Did they play mostly things from music? Did they play waltzes and everything else too? Or what did they play? They played more waltzes.

Ragtime or what? They played ragtime, they played the waltzes, they played the shallots, well the shallots died out. Yeah. But they played the waltzes, they played the reels as much. That was really good. All that kind of stuff.
Did they play them just straight the way they were written or did they sort of add something
to it?
They played the waltzes, they were written.

In fact, the old musician played more music than the younger music playing today because the music got easier. If you take the music, if they put up there the old time from the Red Book and all that, put that old stuff up there. It ain't as jazzy but you can see where the clarinet and things is doing a lot of hard work and if you give it to these fellas what you think is so hot is all that, you put them on some of that music and you see what will happen. They can't even cut it. They can't cut it, they got to practice that stuff. Practice it day and night to get that stuff. It's just like they playing Overture, like they playing Potent Pleasant or either Simaramedy. See all that stuff is hard music. It's rote that way because the man didn't have nobody listen. Now they listen at the thing, they catch it but you have to play what you see.
What were the very best bands you heard in the old days that you would like to listen to? Yeah, or dance bands. When I was a kid?

Yeah. Well I liked the Olympia band. I liked the- Was that with Freddie Keppard? That's Freddie Keppard and I liked the Manuel Perez band. All them bands could play, they all was good. The Olympia band, the Superior band, the Imperial band, all those things. We would play out to the lake, I swear. Now you call me a lie. I shouldn't even say that.
No, I've heard other people, they all got that too out of the lake.

We would go to Canal Street here to catch the Spanish Pro train and if I had to get out there for eight o'clock to play, I'd leave six o'clock in the morning to try to get on that train because I would not get out to the lake two hours ahead of time because they had more drums and basses in their baggage, a whole car full of them and some had to put them in front, some that can't catch that train, catch the next one. Mill and Boyd, you go the same way. In the vision field. Yeah, the same way. It was always packed and they run every fifteen minutes but still you couldn't get on that train.
So many bands working out.

All on the lake, it was just like, take one walk here and it spread like that way. Yeah, I've seen pictures of that. That walk spread that way, it would go to a whole lot of camp. This and everyone, they start that way, they spread out all over the lake, none but can, Bucktown. You go to West End and Mill and Boyd, catch the train and you go to West End and go to Mill and go to West, then we go to Spanish folk. Then we go to Mill and Boyd, then we go to another place further down, I forgot what they called Seabrook. But I'm telling you, you just could pick up your horn and walk out there and the man be running behind you to come and play for you. Then we go on those boats and play on the lake. Every little, like you had a bunch with a boat. I mean a boat from across the street.
They go out on the boats and they.

Yeah, they see boats coming across the street. It was just that big. For them little boats. About 30 feet long. They got about 25, 30 people on the boat. and we sitting up there big and we're playing and it's going over the lake and come back. When that boat go over the lake and come back, it's time to go home. We got to go on another job. And that's the way those boats and they have about two, three hundred of them doggone boats. They all got bands on them. They ain't worried. Oh yeah, they got them little boats and they ain't got nothing with all them different camps. Camps, those people, it's got all those factors and everything they give their dances and things on the lake. It's a pack of people. So many bands, people, you know, they wouldn't even think of musicians you'll see out there. All kind of bands. They had a boy called James Williams, a good band that played from uptown. His dad was named Jim Williams. He played with that Excelsior band. He was a nice band that played. Mud Carey was all right. You heard him, huh?
I knew him. He played with Ory out in California.
Yeah, we played right here and he used to play right there too.
I never knew his brother Jack the trombone band.

Jack used to play trombone. I played with Blind Charlie. A fella called Blind Charlie. He played, he played clarinet, he played piano. He played, he didn't play no saxophone, but clarinet, he played piano. He played guitar. You know what all that means, you know.
He played with Louie Dumaine. He might have heard him with Louie.

He played with Amos Riley, uptown Amos Riley. And so he could take his watch out, the face was broke. So come on, we ain't got about a minute to catch this call. Come on, we got one minute. When he feel like watch the face was open, you could tell the time. I learned a little blind boy, he was sitting there how to play, not clarinet, I learned him how to play saxophone. And he was out in Baton Rouge, he was going to school and he was a great clarinet player. I called him Sidney. Good saxophone player. I know about clarinet, but he got him a clarinet anyhow. He'd play around the boy up on the street so I haven't heard no more about him. He might be dead too. But all those fellas were good musicians around here. The best band named Piro Sapiro's band, those bands was bang. Those were great days. Yeah. Uh-oh.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.

segments.chapter: Louis Dumaine and Kid Rene bands
segments.title: Tape start
segments.summary: Fema recorded announcement; Bill Russell resumes the interview after a break, returning to the Louis Dumaine band.

segments.chapter: Louis Dumaine and Kid Rene bands
segments.title: Louis Dumaine band: Gabriel's music library and its members
segments.summary: Gabriel owned the sheet music so he was hired for the Dumaine band; he names the sidemen and describes the saxophone audition, his brothers and Percy in Detroit.

segments.chapter: Louis Dumaine and Kid Rene bands
segments.title: Buying a saxophone and splitting the tips at the cabaret
segments.summary: Gabriel gets a saxophone on credit, passes the audition, and makes a rule for sharing the singers' tips at the Franklin and Iberville cabaret.

segments.chapter: Louis Dumaine and Kid Rene bands
segments.title: Kid Rene's band at Beansy's club with George Lewis
segments.summary: Beansy and partners offer Gabriel a job; he brings in Kid Rene's band, listing its members including George Lewis and pianist Edna Mitchell.

segments.chapter: Louis Dumaine and Kid Rene bands
segments.title: Pay disputes and Gabriel's large family
segments.summary: George Lewis's wife signs contracts and pays the men; Rene is always owing. Gabriel notes his eleven children and puts his brother August in the band.

segments.chapter: Louis Dumaine and Kid Rene bands
segments.title: The Alley club by St. Bernard market
segments.summary: Interviewer asks about the Alley: a single small hole-in-the-wall club where Rene's band played.

segments.chapter: Louis Dumaine and Kid Rene bands
segments.title: Gabriel's own band at the Pelican: Cecile, Clarence, August and others
segments.summary: He forms a band with his sister Cecile, brothers Clarence and August, and sidemen like Eddie Summers, George McCullum, Gilbert Young and Sidney Fleuja.

segments.chapter: Louis Dumaine and Kid Rene bands
segments.title: Finding Gilbert Young and warning about a local
segments.summary: They discuss where Gilbert Young can be found and a side remark about a personal relationship.

segments.chapter: Gabriel's sons, small bands and Detroit
segments.title: Teaching his sons trumpet and leading a big band
segments.summary: Gabriel teaches his sons Morton and August trumpet using what he learned from old man Delmore, and runs a big band with his sons and nephew.

segments.chapter: Gabriel's sons, small bands and Detroit
segments.title: Small bands with Dave Foster and Clifford Brown, and clarinet picnic trios
segments.summary: He remembers a five-piece band with singer Joe Morris and picnic jobs with clarinet, bass and banjo, where Elliot Taylor subbed for him.

segments.chapter: Gabriel's sons, small bands and Detroit
segments.title: Working in Detroit in a Dixieland band
segments.summary: Gabriel talks about the Detroit Dixieland band, saxophone versus clarinet, a letter about a World's Fair job, and the pay offered.

segments.chapter: Gabriel's sons, small bands and Detroit
segments.title: Detroit sons and two years at the Parkland Hotel
segments.summary: He says he never stopped playing, mentions his son Charles, and a two-year Dixieland engagement at the Parkland Hotel.

segments.chapter: Keppard, Oliver and old-timers
segments.title: Freddie Keppard: early violin, trumpet lessons, Chicago
segments.summary: Gabriel knew Freddie Keppard as a violinist who played with his father, took trumpet lessons, and went to Chicago in 1910.

segments.chapter: Keppard, Oliver and old-timers
segments.title: Armstrong's last dance, Sidney Desvigne's band and King Oliver
segments.summary: Gabriel recalls Armstrong's farewell dance in 1923, playing drums in Sidney Desvigne's band, and King Oliver rehearsing with his father.

segments.chapter: Keppard, Oliver and old-timers
segments.title: Old-time players and George McCullum Sr.'s cornet
segments.summary: Talk of old George McCullum, his widow keeping his cornet, and Gabriel's own E-flat and B-flat cornets and clarinet in Detroit.

segments.chapter: Parade bands, instruments and the Eureka band
segments.title: Playing in the Eureka band
segments.summary: Gabriel says he was a member of the Eureka band with T-Boy, playing saxophone, drums or clarinet as needed.

segments.chapter: Parade bands, instruments and the Eureka band
segments.title: Albert-system clarinets, E-flats and buffets
segments.summary: They discuss Albert-system clarinets, tone, his German E-flat, buffet clarinets, and missing a parade.

segments.chapter: Parade bands, instruments and the Eureka band
segments.title: WPA band and the Chum Club with T-Boy
segments.summary: Gabriel names the musicians in his WPA-era band and at Babe Carous's Chum Club.

segments.chapter: Parade bands, instruments and the Eureka band
segments.title: Eureka band members: trombones, bass, drummers
segments.summary: Gabriel and the interviewer sort out the Eureka band's trombonists, bassists, baritone player and its drummers.

segments.chapter: Parade bands, instruments and the Eureka band
segments.title: The record band, trumpet section and the scab band charge
segments.summary: Gabriel describes the record band's trumpeters and why Clayton was not used, and how it was a scab band while he held a union card.

segments.chapter: Rudolph's band, Joe Petit and the voice band
segments.title: Band with Sidney Fluesa, Rudolph and Gilbert Young
segments.summary: He lists a six-piece band with Rudolph, Al Seed, Sidney Fluesa, Gilbert Young and two trombonists named Morris French.

segments.chapter: Rudolph's band, Joe Petit and the voice band
segments.title: Joe Petit and Ambrose, trombonists
segments.summary: Gabriel recalls playing with Joe Petit, who played trombone without teeth, Buddy Petit's stepfather, and violinist-turned-trombonist Ambrose.

segments.chapter: Rudolph's band, Joe Petit and the voice band
segments.title: The Louis Armstrong vocal band and Louis Prevost
segments.summary: He lists the members of the band with Armstrong including Joe Lindsay and Louis Prevost, a fine clarinetist.

segments.chapter: Clarinetists and Maurice Durand's band
segments.title: Best clarinet players Gabriel heard
segments.summary: Asked for his favourite clarinetists, Gabriel names T.O. and others like Sam Dutrey, Louis Nelson and Lawrence Dewey.

segments.chapter: Clarinetists and Maurice Durand's band
segments.title: Wade, Johnny Dodds, Georgie Boy and Jimmy Noone
segments.summary: They discuss Wade's playing, Dodds and Bechet-style players, and Jimmy Newton known as Jimbo.

segments.chapter: Clarinetists and Maurice Durand's band
segments.title: Playing drums in Maurice Durand's band
segments.summary: Gabriel joined Maurice Durand's reading band on drums, lists its members, and recalls Durand's later move to California.

segments.chapter: Clarinetists and Maurice Durand's band
segments.title: Horse Minetta, multi-instrumentalist
segments.summary: Gabriel praises Horse who could play two trombones at once and any instrument, and mentions his own recent playing.

segments.chapter: Clarinetists and Maurice Durand's band
segments.title: More on T.O.'s clarinet playing
segments.summary: Why Gabriel rates T.O. so high, and Donnell Howard's remark in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Trumpet players of the old days
segments.title: Wooden Joe, Willie Phillip and Frank Keeling
segments.summary: Early trumpeters in Gabriel's father's band, with Frank Keeling remembered as a fighter.

segments.chapter: Trumpet players of the old days
segments.title: Jimmy Strode, old man Barbarin and the DuPas brothers
segments.summary: Brief remarks on Jimmy Strode, Barbarin, and Dave and Rudolph DuPas.

segments.chapter: Trumpet players of the old days
segments.title: Gabriel's six musical sons
segments.summary: Gabriel names his sons and what each plays.

segments.chapter: Trumpet players of the old days
segments.title: Joe Johnson, Chip and Tick Chambers
segments.summary: Talk of trumpeters Joe Johnson, Lee Collins's wrestling, Chip, Jesse and Tick Chambers.

segments.chapter: Trumpet players of the old days
segments.title: Sugar Johnny, Roy Palmer, Harrison Ball and Sam Baldwin
segments.summary: Gabriel describes trumpeters Sugar Johnny, Roy Palmer, Harrison Ball, and Sam Baldwin's band.

segments.chapter: Trumpet players of the old days
segments.title: Favourite trumpeters: Manuel Perez, Oliver, Keppard and Kid Rene
segments.summary: Gabriel prefers Manuel Perez, compares Perez, Oliver and Keppard, and Rene's tone.

segments.chapter: Dance bands and the lakefront
segments.title: What old dance bands played
segments.summary: Old dance bands played ragtime, waltzes and reels as written; Gabriel argues older music was harder.

segments.chapter: Dance bands and the lakefront
segments.title: Bands and boats on Lake Pontchartrain
segments.summary: Gabriel recalls the best bands and crowded trains and boats of the lakefront resorts.

segments.title: Mud Carey, Jack, and Blind Charlie
segments.summary: Brief recollections of Mud Carey, his brother Jack, and Blind Charlie, whom he taught saxophone.
